Introduction

german_name.evidence_anchor:
Nixon (1980) presented evidence which showed that the commercial landings of es tuarine-dependent species on a unit area basis are correlated with the ratio marsh area/ open water area among the major regions of the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts with one notable exception. The Chesapeake Bay has the highest yield of commercial species (kg/
ha) but a rather low marsh to open water ratio. Although such comparisons are made difficult because of the less well bounded nature of the other coastal systems (they do not contain as much open water), more liberal inclusion ofnearshore waters in the calculations for the other regions would only exaggerate the discrepency. Nixon further demonstrated that other coastal ecosystems removed from wetlands have commercial finfish and shellfish yields exceeding those of estuaries which include a large marsh area. The high fishery productivity reported by Nixon for the Chesapeake Bay is substantially due to menhaden _(Brevoortia_ spp.), which dominate fishery biomass on both Atlantic and Gulf Coasts.

The findings about overall increases in benthic macrofauna biomass are consistent with those of other
organically enriched North Sea areas (intertidal: see
BEUKEMA & CADCE, 1986 and also REISE & SCHUBERT,
1987; subtidal: see ROSENBERG et al., 1987, for eastern
Skagerrak and DUINEVELD et al., 1987 for _Amphiura_
populations in the offshore North Sea); they are also
in agreement and comparable with findings from other
areas, e.g. the Kattegat (PEARSON et al., 1985). While
a great variety of short-lived, adaptive species may profit
from organic enrichment at the sediment-water interface in
eutrophicated areas and thus contribute to the
overall increases in biomass (and even more in productivity),
specialized and long-lived species will slowly
become less important and will even vanish. Such effects
are to be expected especially in environments
which are over-burdened with organic matter and
where, due to hydrographic conditions, during calm
summer weather, oxygen in the bottom habitat may
become deficient; sub-surface dwelling macrofauna will
be extinguished first in such environments as shown
for the mud area of the inner German Bight. All these
findings are indications that the bottom
microfauna of the German Bight is strongly influenced
by increased eutrophication and, hence, organic enrichment
of the bottom sediments. In spite of the high
natural variability of the faunal assemblages and their
adaptability to changes, effects have become
recognizable, among which the increased biomass and
shifts in dominances in favour of adaptive, short-lived
(and hence highly productive) species are the most obvious.
Only a few examples have been presented until now which
point to a gradual disappearance of less
adaptive faunal elements in the inner Bight (HEIBER &
RACHOR, 1989).

CONCLUSIONS


Microorganisms are vital to all ecosystems, but our
knowledge about the relationship between their diversity
and ecosystem productivity is still poor. Although controlled experiments can provide mechanistic insight into
diversity-productivity-relationships, results are rarely
directly applicable to complex natural ecosystems, such
as marine coastal environments. Our field campaign on
a heterogeneous sedimentary seafloor revealed the
importance of microorganisms for aquatic ecosystems
and showed that diatom diversity most likely forms the
lowest boundary for ecosystem productivity. To our
knowledge, this result has not previously been observed.
